newsitem.title: CANADA: Thin majority to challenge Canada's Chretien.
newsitem.headline: Thin majority to challenge Canada's Chretien.

text.p: Prime Minister Jean Chretien may have won a new parliamentary majority in Monday's election, but the margin was so thin that he will have a tough battle facing down conflicting pressures from the left and right.
Chretien's Liberals took 155 of 301 seats in the House of Commons on Monday, down from 177 of 295 in 1993.

The Liberals would slip into a minority if they lost five members of Parliament in their five-year mandate. Restive backbenchers in Chretien's party could also pose serious problems for controversial legislation he might seek to pass.
Chretien on Tuesday brushed aside such concerns, noting he had served in minority governments and that a thin majority was easy by comparison.

"When you have a majority, and you have four parties, located in different parts of Canada, with some on the right, some extreme right, some at the left, you know, it's not a difficult political problem," he declared.

The prime minister's spokesman, Peter Donolo, said that in the last Parliament the government sometimes won the support of other parties, including the separatist Bloc Quebecois and right-wing Reform Party, and could now turn to four parties for support.
But Chretien faces new difficulties with his sharply reduced majority.

On the left, he must deal with a reinvigorated New Democratic Party (NDP), which rose to 21 seats from nine and toppled two cabinet ministers and numerous other Liberal members of Parliament, especially in economically depressed Atlantic Canada.

The separatist Bloc Quebecois, led by ex-Communist Gilles Duceppe, also questions government spending cuts, and even the Conservative Party, which jumped to 20 seats from just two, could pose a challenge on the left.
The Conservatives, despite officially advocating tax and selected spending cuts, ran to the fiscal left of the Liberals in Atlantic Canada, where they picked up most of their seats.
Chretien said it was clear the maritime provinces had expressed their displeasure with measures he said had been necessary, such as tightening unemployment insurance rules.
"The cuts hurt in some areas," he said in his hometown of Shawinigan, Quebec, before returning to Ottawa.
Treasury Board President Marcel Masse, while awaiting Chretien's arrival in Ottawa, told reporters there would be renewed pressure for spending on social programs.
"In the Atlantic provinces, I think the message was clear, that we have cut enough in terms of the social programs and it's time to look at ways to improve them," he said.
Masse said it was important to finish the job of eliminating Canada's deficit, but that afterward it would be possible to look at new spending or tax reductions.
Meanwhile, the voice on the right was strengthened as Reform replaced the Bloc as the official opposition.
Reform, which almost swept the western provinces of British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan, was seen pressing the Liberals to cut taxes rather than spend any budget surplus.

The divisions in Parliament are aggravated by the parties' regional makeup -- the Conservatives mainly in the East, the Bloc Quebecois in Quebec, the Liberals concentrated in Ontario and Reform in the West, with the NDP scattered across Canada.
Chretien also faces possible rumblings over his leadership. Some media commentators have begun to ask whether he should step down, but he has pledged to serve his full mandate.
